title: Radha goes to him
hookLine: Radha's friend says she's held on long enough, and Radha walks through the dark to Krishna
carry: smarana: bring the beloved back to mind

cards: Radha has sent him away. Now her friend sits with her in the bower and says it plainly: you've held on to your anger long enough.
Then Krishna himself comes back and pleads with her, the Lord of the world asking his beloved to forgive him. And the friend says it once more: go. He's waiting in the grove by the river.
So Radha goes, slowly, a little shy, through the dark trees. In the poem's last songs they're together at last, and she asks him to set her ornaments straight, and he does.

teach.b: Look back over the week and one thing keeps happening: somebody is remembering somebody. Krishna by the river keeps seeing Radha's face. Radha can't look at the moon without thinking of him.

At dawn, every sharp word she says is about him. Nobody in this poem forgets, and that's why they find each other again. Jayadeva named it before the story began: if your heart is moved by remembering Hari, listen.
Remembering is smarana. In the Bhagavata, the boy Prahlada lists the ways of devotion, and among them are hearing about Vishnu, singing about him, and remembering him.
There, remembering isn't something that happens to you. It's something you do: bring the beloved back to mind, again and again, in the middle of ordinary life.
That's why Hindus repeat a divine name on a mala, sing kirtan, and tell the same stories every year though everyone knows the ending.

And it's why the Gita Govinda has been sung in worship at Puri for centuries: singing it is remembering Hari. Every dancer who walks Radha to the grove is doing what the poem asked for in its first lines.
Just before the Gita Govinda, Sudama's rice went on the tray.

teach.h: AN OFFERING THAT NEEDS NO TRAY.
teach.b: Smarana is an offering that needs no tray.
The hands can be still while the mind brings the beloved back.

how: In bhakti traditions, smarana, remembering the deity, is practiced through repeating a divine name (often on a mala), singing, and hearing stories; Vaishnava devotees sing and dance the Gita Govinda's songs, and it has long been sung in worship at the Jagannath temple in Puri.

o: a calm mind emptied of every face and name
the duty of serving a teacher with your hands
devotion that keeps bringing the beloved back to mind

games.q: the end of the poem — tap the pairs.
p: you've held on long enough: go

s: in the Gita Govinda's week of scenes, the lovers manage to forget each other for a while
Krishna sees Radha's face, the moon reminds Radha of him, and her anger at dawn is all about him.
in the Bhagavata, Prahlada names remembering among the ways of devotion
with hearing about Vishnu and singing about him.
the poem ends with Radha and Krishna still apart
her friend coaxes her, Krishna comes back and pleads, and Radha goes to him.

games.q: you sit down to practice smarana, and the mind wanders off to a shopping list. what do you do?
o: give up. the sit is ruined.
force the mind to stay perfectly still.
notice, and let the beloved come back to mind.
games.why: smarana is letting the beloved come back to mind, again and again, in the middle of ordinary life.

practice: If you pray, choose a name you already use, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, the Mother, and let it rest in the mind with each breath, the way people count a name on a mala. If you don't, bring to mind the face of someone you love.
When the mind drifts, notice where it went, and bring the name or the face back, gently. That return is the practice, the same one Radha and Krishna kept all week.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion. This week the Gita Govinda showed it as the Lord close enough to love, longing on both sides, honest anger, and smarana, remembering the beloved again and again.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: smarana, remembering. In bhakti, letting the beloved come back to mind, again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: smarana, bring the beloved back to mind. That's the last of our Gita Govinda days. Until tomorrow.
